title: Blood Supply, Veins and Lymphatics of the Lower Limb
introduction: The lower limb is supplied primarily by the continuation of the external iliac artery as the femoral artery, supplemented by branches of the internal iliac artery[cite: 137]. Venous return and fluid homeostasis are maintained by superficial and deep venous systems equipped with valves alongside superficial and deep lymphatic channels that filter lymph through the popliteal and inguinal lymph nodes[cite: 137].
learningOutcomes: 6.1 Trace the main arterial pathway of the lower limb from the abdominal aorta and iliac arteries to the plantar and dorsalis pedis arteries[cite: 137].
6.2 Describe the course, relations, and major branches of the femoral artery, including the profunda femoris artery[cite: 137].
6.3 Locate the clinical palpation sites for the femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis pulses and note normal anatomical variation[cite: 137].
6.4 Differentiate the superficial, perforating, and deep veins of the lower limb and explain the mechanism of varicose veins[cite: 137].
6.5 Outline the superficial and deep lymph nodes and lymphatic vessels of the lower limb along with the clinical significance of inguinal lymphadenopathy[cite: 137].

content.heading: Arterial Supply of the Lower Limb
content.body: At the level of L4, the abdominal aorta divides into the right and left common iliac arteries, each of which divides into external and internal iliac arteries[cite: 137]. The internal iliac artery contributes to lower limb blood supply via branches such as the superior gluteal, inferior gluteal, and obturator arteries[cite: 137]. The external iliac artery passes behind the inguinal ligament to become the femoral artery, the primary blood supply to the entire lower limb[cite: 137]. At the adductor hiatus (opening in the adductor magnus), the femoral artery becomes the popliteal artery, which terminates at the lower border of the popliteus muscle by dividing into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries[cite: 137]. The anterior tibial artery supplies the anterior compartment of the leg and terminates anterior to the ankle joint as the dorsalis pedis artery[cite: 137]. The posterior tibial artery supplies the posterior and lateral compartments of the leg and ends deep to the flexor retinaculum by dividing into the medial and lateral plantar arteries supplying the sole[cite: 137].

content.heading: Course and Branches of the Femoral Artery
content.body: The femoral artery enters the thigh behind the inguinal ligament at the midinguinal point, midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the symphysis pubis[cite: 137]. As it descends, its upper half lies superficially within the femoral triangle, whereas its lower half runs deeply within the subsartorial (adductor) canal[cite: 137]. It descends almost vertically toward the adductor tubercle of the femur before passing through the adductor hiatus into the popliteal space as the popliteal artery[cite: 137]. Its major branch, the profunda femoris artery (deep artery of the thigh), arises from the lateral side of the femoral artery about 4 cm below the inguinal ligament and gives off the lateral femoral circumflex artery, medial femoral circumflex artery, and perforating arteries[cite: 137].

content.heading: Palpation of Lower Limb Arterial Pulses
content.body: The femoral pulse is easily palpated in the femoral triangle just inferior to the inguinal ligament, midway between the pubic symphysis and the anterior superior iliac spine[cite: 137]. The popliteal pulse is difficult to find but can usually be detected on deep palpation just medial to the midline of the popliteal fossa[cite: 137]. The posterior tibial pulse is palpable just posteroinferior to the medial malleolus, between the calcaneal tendon (heel) and the medial malleolus[cite: 137]. The dorsalis pedis pulse is felt on the dorsum of the foot over the tarsal bones, where the artery lies parallel and between the tendon of extensor hallucis longus and the tendon of extensor digitorum longus to the second toe[cite: 137]. Clinically, the dorsalis pedis artery may be congenitally absent or nonpalpable in about 15% of people (usually bilaterally), in which case it is replaced by an enlarged perforating fibular artery[cite: 137].

content.heading: Superficial and Perforating Veins of the Lower Limb
content.body: Lower limb veins are divided into superficial and deep groups, both containing valves that are more numerous in the deep veins[cite: 137]. The two major superficial veins run in the superficial fascia (subcutaneous tissue): the great saphenous vein and the small saphenous vein[cite: 137]. The great saphenous vein is the longest vein in the body; it starts at the medial end of the dorsal venous arch uniting with the dorsal vein of the great toe, ascends about 2.5 cm anterior to the medial malleolus, passes posterior to the medial femoral condyle (a hand's breadth behind the medial border of the patella), traverses the saphenous opening in the fascia lata, and empties into the femoral vein immediately below the inguinal ligament[cite: 137]. Its tributaries include the posterior arch vein, lateral and medial accessory saphenous veins, superficial circumflex iliac vein, superficial external pudendal vein, and superficial epigastric vein[cite: 137]. The small saphenous vein arises from the dorsal venous arch and dorsal vein of the little toe, ascends posterior to the lateral malleolus along the lateral border of the calcaneal tendon, penetrates the deep fascia to ascend between the heads of gastrocnemius, and empties into the popliteal vein in the popliteal fossa[cite: 137]. Perforating veins pierce the deep fascia to connect superficial and deep veins via unidirectional valves essential for normal drainage[cite: 137].

content.heading: Deep Veins and Venous Clinical Correlates
content.body: Deep veins lie beneath the deep fascia within the same vascular sheath as their corresponding arteries so arterial pulsations assist venous return, and are grouped into veins of the foot, leg, knee, and thigh[cite: 137]. In the foot, plantar digital veins continue into plantar metatarsal veins and the plantar venous arch alongside dorsal veins[cite: 137]. In the leg, medial and lateral plantar veins form the posterior tibial and fibular (peroneal) veins behind the malleoli, which together with the anterior tibial vein drain into the popliteal vein behind the knee[cite: 137]. The popliteal vein is formed by the union of the anterior and posterior tibial veins, has 4 or 5 valves, receives the small saphenous vein, lies medial to the popliteal artery distally between the gastrocnemius heads, and pierces adductor magnus proximally to become the femoral vein[cite: 137]. The femoral vein continues directly from the popliteal vein deep in the thigh and is a common clinical site for venous catheterization and blood sampling because it provides direct access to the right atrium of the heart[cite: 137]. Clinically, incompetent venous valves cause retrograde blood flow and varicose veins, most commonly affecting the great saphenous vein and its tributaries[cite: 137].

content.heading: Lymphatic Drainage of the Lower Limb
content.body: The lymphatic system returns tissue fluid and plasma proteins (slightly alkaline transudative lymph) to the bloodstream and supports immune defense[cite: 137]. Superficial inguinal lymph nodes (more than 10 nodes in the upper femoral triangle) are subdivided into an upper horizontal group (5 or more nodes below the inguinal ligament draining the anterior abdominal wall below the umbilicus, gluteal region below the iliac crest, superficial perineum, and lower half of the anal canal) and a lower vertical group (up to 4 nodes below the saphenous opening draining superficial lower leg structures except the lateral foot and back of the leg)[cite: 137]. Deep lymph nodes comprise deep inguinal nodes (along the femoral vein draining superficial inguinal and popliteal nodes), popliteal nodes (3 to 6 nodes in the popliteal fossa draining the skin of the lateral foot and back of the leg, deep leg and foot structures, and knee lymphatics), and variably present anterior tibial nodes (on the upper anterior tibial artery draining the anterior leg into popliteal nodes)[cite: 137]. Superficial lymphatic vessels divide into medial vessels (following the great saphenous vein to the sub-inguinal nodes) and lateral vessels (following the small saphenous vein to the popliteal nodes or crossing below the knee to join the medial group), while fewer deep vessels follow the anterior tibial, posterior tibial, and peroneal arteries into popliteal nodes[cite: 137]. Clinically, enlarged inguinal lymph nodes (lymphadenopathy) reflect abnormalities in size, number, or consistency typically due to infection, malignancy, or autoimmune disease[cite: 137].

inTextQuestions.question: At what anatomical landmark does the femoral artery end and become the popliteal artery?
inTextQuestions.answer: At the adductor hiatus (opening in the adductor magnus muscle)[cite: 137].

inTextQuestions.question: Approximately what percentage of people have a congenitally absent or nonpalpable dorsalis pedis artery, and which vessel replaces it?
inTextQuestions.answer: Around 15% of people, in whom the dorsalis pedis artery is replaced by an enlarged perforating fibular artery[cite: 137].

inTextQuestions.question: Where do the great saphenous vein and the small saphenous vein terminate?
inTextQuestions.answer: The great saphenous vein traverses the saphenous opening to empty into the femoral vein just below the inguinal ligament, whereas the small saphenous vein empties into the popliteal vein in the popliteal fossa[cite: 137].

inTextQuestions.question: Which two superficial areas of the lower leg and foot drain into the popliteal lymph nodes rather than the vertical group of superficial inguinal nodes?
inTextQuestions.answer: The lateral side of the foot and the back of the leg[cite: 137].

saqs.question: Trace the main arterial continuity from the abdominal aorta at L4 to the sole and dorsum of the foot.
saqs.answer: The abdominal aorta divides at L4 into common iliac arteries, which split into external and internal iliac arteries[cite: 137]. The external iliac artery becomes the femoral artery behind the inguinal ligament, continues as the popliteal artery at the adductor hiatus, and divides at the lower border of popliteus into the anterior tibial artery (becoming the dorsalis pedis artery in front of the ankle) and posterior tibial artery (dividing deep to the flexor retinaculum into the medial and lateral plantar arteries)[cite: 137].

saqs.question: State the exact clinical sites for palpating the femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis pulses.
saqs.answer: Femoral pulse: just below the inguinal ligament midway between the pubic symphysis and anterior superior iliac spine[cite: 137]. Popliteal pulse: deep palpation just medial to the midline of the popliteal fossa[cite: 137]. Posterior tibial pulse: just posteroinferior to the medial malleolus between the heel and medial malleolus[cite: 137]. Dorsalis pedis pulse: on the dorsum of the foot between and parallel to the tendons of extensor hallucis longus and extensor digitorum longus to the second toe[cite: 137].

saqs.question: Describe the origin, course, and termination of the great saphenous vein, and list its major tributaries.
saqs.answer: The great saphenous vein starts at the medial end of the dorsal venous arch uniting with the dorsal vein of the great toe, ascends about 2.5 cm anterior to the medial malleolus, passes posterior to the medial femoral condyle, traverses the saphenous opening in the fascia lata, and empties into the femoral vein immediately below the inguinal ligament[cite: 137]. Its tributaries are the posterior arch vein, lateral and medial accessory saphenous veins, superficial circumflex iliac vein, superficial external pudendal vein, and superficial epigastric vein[cite: 137].

saqs.question: Explain why the femoral vein is commonly used for venous catheterization and define varicose veins.
saqs.answer: The femoral vein is a large deep thigh vessel frequently chosen for catheterization and venous sampling because it offers easy access to the right atrium of the heart[cite: 137]. Varicose veins occur when venous valves become incompetent, causing retrograde flow of blood—most commonly affecting the great saphenous vein and its tributaries[cite: 137].

saqs.question: Differentiate the drainage territories of the upper horizontal superficial inguinal lymph nodes, lower vertical superficial inguinal lymph nodes, and popliteal lymph nodes.
saqs.answer: The upper horizontal superficial inguinal nodes drain the anterior abdominal wall below the umbilicus, gluteal region below the iliac crest, superficial perineum, and lower half of the anal canal[cite: 137]. The lower vertical superficial inguinal nodes drain superficial structures of the lower leg except the lateral side of the foot and back of the leg[cite: 137]. The popliteal lymph nodes drain the skin and subcutaneous tissue of the lateral side of the foot and back of the leg, deep structures of the leg and foot, and knee lymphatics[cite: 137].
